entry: Nontrinitarian movement of [[Christianity]] affirming the unitary nature of God as a single, unique creator. Unitarians reject the [[Trinity]] as a later theological corruption, and most regard [[Jesus]] as a moral and spiritual teacher subordinate to God. Accordingly, they reject the ecumenical councils and creeds. The movement emerged during the Radical Reformation in the mid-16th century, in the [[Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth]] and in [[Transylvania]], where Ferenc Dávid founded the Unitarian Church of Transylvania. Repression in 17th-century Poland led many Unitarians to flee or be killed. In England, the first Unitarian church opened in 1774 on Essex Street, London. The first North American congregation to accept the faith was King's Chapel in [[Boston]], where James Freeman began teaching Unitarian doctrine in 1784. Unitarianism is not a single denomination but a collection of existing and extinct groups that share belief in God's unity.

[[Sovereign state]] governed as a single entity, in which the central government holds supreme authority. The central government may create or abolish sub-national divisions and decides which powers to delegate to them. It may alter the statute that devolves power, overriding or expanding the authority of devolved governments. The concept originated in [[France]], where national feeling after the [[Hundred Years' War]] unified the country and transformed it from a feudal monarchy. Conquests during and after the [[Napoleonic Wars]] and the vast [[French colonial empire]] spread the model. Unitary states contrast with [[Federation|federations]], whose constituent units hold powers that the central government cannot unilaterally change. About 166 of the 193 UN member countries have unitary systems, though federations cover a significant share of the world's population and land. The [[United Kingdom]], Spain and China are examples.

Major U.S. airline headquartered in [[Chicago]], [[Illinois]]. It operates an extensive domestic and international network across the United States and to destinations on six continents. Regional service is provided by independent carriers under the United Express brand. United was one of the five founding members of the Star Alliance, which extends its network worldwide. William E. Boeing, founder of the Boeing Aircraft Company in 1916, launched an air service between Victoria, [[British Columbia]], and [[Seattle]]. He later acquired three more airlines, completing a merger by 1931 that formed United Air Lines.

Federal semi-constitutional monarchy of seven emirates in [[West Asia]], at the eastern end of the [[Arabian Peninsula]]. [[Abu Dhabi]] is the capital and [[Dubai]] the largest city. Islam is the state religion, and only 11% of the population are native Emiratis. After piracy prompted British intervention in the 19th century, local sheikhdoms formed the Trucial States, a British protectorate. The Trucial States gained full independence as the UAE in 1971. Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan, ruler of Abu Dhabi and the first president (1971–2004), invested oil revenues in healthcare, education and infrastructure. The country is a member of the [[United Nations]], and Dubai is a major hub of finance, tourism and commerce. Human rights organizations consider the UAE substandard, citing reports of government critics being imprisoned and tortured.

American multinational corporation that traded tropical fruit, chiefly [[Banana|bananas]], grown on Latin American plantations. It was formed in 1899 from the merger of the Boston Fruit Company with Minor C. Keith's banana-trading enterprises. It controlled vast territories and transportation networks in Central America, the Caribbean coast of [[Colombia]] and the West Indies. It held a near-monopoly in some regions, later called banana republics, such as [[Costa Rica]], [[Honduras]] and [[Guatemala]]. Critics accused it of exploitative neocolonialism. After financial decline, it merged with Eli M. Black's AMK in 1970 as United Brands, which Carl Lindner Jr. renamed Chiquita Brands International in 1984.

headword: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland
sort_key: united kingdom of great britain and ireland
entry: Unitary sovereign state formed by the Acts of Union in 1801, joining the [[Kingdom of Great Britain]] and the Kingdom of Ireland. The [[Royal Navy]] helped the [[British Empire]] become the foremost world power. The Great Irish Famine, worsened by government inaction, caused demographic collapse in much of Ireland. [[Canada]], [[Australia]], New Zealand, Newfoundland and South Africa became self-governing dominions. Britain fought in [[World War I]] against the [[Central Powers]]. The Irish War of Independence led to recognition of the Irish Free State in 1922, and in 1927 the state was renamed the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland.

Principal organ of the [[United Nations]] responsible for international peace and security. It may authorize peacekeeping operations, military action and sanctions, and its resolutions bind all member states. Its five permanent members, [[China]], France, [[Russia]], the [[United Kingdom]] and the [[United States]], each hold veto power over substantive resolutions. Created in 1945 to succeed the [[League of Nations]], the council first met in 1946. Rivalry during the [[Cold War]] largely paralyzed it, but peacekeeping expanded after the [[Soviet Union]] dissolved in 1991. In the 2020s, vetoes by Russia over Ukraine and by the United States over Gaza have renewed paralysis.

Combined military forces of the [[United States]]. Federal law establishes six armed forces: the Army, Marine Corps, Navy, Air Force, Space Force and Coast Guard. The Coast Guard serves under the Department of Homeland Security in peacetime. The Army and Navy were established during the [[American Revolutionary War]] and later played decisive roles in conflicts including the [[War of 1812]], [[World War I]], [[World War II]], the [[Cold War]] and the [[War on terror]]. The force has been all-volunteer since 1973. The Space Force, created in 2019, is the newest branch.

First ten amendments to the [[Constitution of the United States]]. Written to address objections raised by Anti-Federalists during the 1787–88 ratification debate, they were largely the work of [[James Madison]]. Ten amendments were ratified on December 15, 1791. The amendments guarantee freedoms of speech, religion, press and assembly, the right to keep and bear arms, and protections in criminal procedure. They also reserve powers not granted to the federal government for the states or the people. Many provisions later applied to the states through the Fourteenth Amendment, a process called incorporation. They built on earlier documents such as the [[Magna Carta]].

Neoclassical seat of the [[United States Congress]] in [[Washington, D.C.]] It stands on Capitol Hill at the eastern end of the National Mall and forms the origin point for the district's street-numbering system. The 6th U.S. Congress first convened there on November 17, 1800, after the capital moved from [[Philadelphia]]. British forces partly burned the building in 1814 during the [[War of 1812]], and it was fully restored within five years. The massive dome was completed around 1866, just after the [[American Civil War]]. The west front is used for presidential inaugurations.

Bicameral [[Legislature|legislature]] of the federal government of the United States. Congress has 535 voting members: 100 senators and 435 representatives. The House and Senate both meet in the [[United States Capitol]] in [[Washington, D.C.]] Members are chosen by direct election, though a governor may fill Senate vacancies by appointment. Congresses last two years and begin every other January. Congress was created by Article One of the Constitution and first met in 1789. Since the late 19th century, members have typically belonged to the [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic Party]] or the [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican Party]], though no law requires it.

Founding document of the [[United States]], adopted unanimously in [[Philadelphia]] on July 4, 1776, by the Second Continental Congress. Drafted largely by [[Thomas Jefferson]], it explains why the [[Thirteen Colonies]] regarded themselves as independent sovereign states no longer subject to British rule. It cites 27 colonial grievances against King [[George III]] and asserts natural rights, including a right of revolution. The delegates knew they were committing high treason against the Crown. Most signatures were added on August 2, 1776. [[Abraham Lincoln]] viewed the document as the moral standard for the nation and made it the centerpiece of his [[Gettysburg Address]] in 1863. Its second sentence, asserting that all men are created equal, is considered one of the most famed lines in world history.

Executive department of the federal government that coordinates and supervises the [[United States Armed Forces]]. Also referred to as the Department of War, it is headquartered at the [[The Pentagon|Pentagon]] in Arlington County, Virginia. The secretary of defense, a cabinet-level official, reports directly to the president. The department has three military departments, the Army, Navy and Air Force, and four national intelligence services, including the [[National Security Agency]]. As of November 2022, it had more than 1.4 million active-duty uniformed personnel and more than 747,000 civilian employees. Its mission is "to provide the military forces needed to deter war and ensure our nation's security."

Executive department of the federal government that oversees domestic enforcement of federal laws. Headed by the attorney general, a cabinet member who reports to the [[President of the United States|president]], it contains most federal law enforcement agencies, including the [[Federal Bureau of Investigation]], the U.S. Marshals Service and the Drug Enforcement Administration. Its lawyers represent the federal government through eight litigating divisions, and U.S. attorneys' offices cover each of the 94 federal judicial districts. The office of attorney general dates to the Judiciary Act of 1789, but Congress created the department in 1870 during the presidency of [[Ulysses S. Grant]].

Lower chamber of the bicameral [[United States Congress]]. Its 435 voting seats have been fixed since 1913, except in 1959–63, when the admission of Alaska and Hawaii temporarily raised the total to 437. Members serve two-year terms.Five non-voting delegates represent the District of Columbia and several U.S. territories. The House alone may originate revenue bills, impeach federal officers and elect the president if no candidate wins an Electoral College majority. It meets in the south wing of the [[United States Capitol]]. As of the 2020 census, [[California]] had the largest delegation, with 52 representatives.

Naval infantry service branch of the [[United States Armed Forces]]. Legally part of the Department of the Navy since June 30, 1834, the Corps conducts expeditionary and amphibious warfare with its own infantry, artillery, aviation and special operations forces. Its fighter attack squadrons are embedded in Navy carrier air wings and operate from [[Aircraft carrier|aircraft carriers]]. Two battalions of Continental Marines were formed in [[Philadelphia]] on November 10, 1775. In the Pacific theater of [[World War II]], the Corps led an island-by-island amphibious campaign. As of December 2024, it had about 169,000 active-duty members and some 33,000 reservists.

Federal service academy in West Point, New York, that educates officers for the U.S. Army. Founded in 1802, it is the oldest of the five American service academies. The Army has occupied the site since 1780, when it built a fort during the [[American Revolutionary War]]. Cadets receive a Bachelor of Science degree, and the Army fully funds their tuition in exchange for an active-duty service obligation. It was the first American college with an accredited [[Civil engineering|civil engineering]] program and the first to award class rings. Alumni include presidents [[Ulysses S. Grant]] and [[Dwight D. Eisenhower]] and the Confederate general [[Robert E. Lee]].

Upper house of the bicameral [[United States Congress]]. Each of the 50 states elects two senators to staggered six-year terms, for 100 members. Senators were chosen by state legislatures until 1913, when the Seventeenth Amendment provided for popular election. The Senate has exclusive power to confirm presidential appointments and approve treaties, and it conducts trials of officials [[Impeachment|impeached]] by the House. The vice president presides and votes only when the Senate is evenly divided. A characteristic practice is the filibuster, which can be ended by a vote for cloture.

[[Caribbean]] unincorporated territory of the United States, in the Leeward Islands of the [[Lesser Antilles]]. It consists of Saint Croix, Saint John and Saint Thomas, plus about 50 smaller islands and cays, with a total land area of 133.73 square miles (346.36 sq km). The capital is Charlotte Amalie on Saint Thomas. Previously the Danish West Indies, the islands were sold to the United States for $25 million in the 1917 Treaty of the Danish West Indies. In the 18th and early 19th centuries, [[Sugarcane|sugarcane]] plantations worked by enslaved Africans drove the economy. Tourism and services are the primary economic activities.

Units of measurement used in the [[United States]], derived from English units. The customary system was standardized in 1832 on the basis of the system then in use in the United Kingdom before the imperial system took effect on January 1, 1826. Many units are similar to their [[Imperial units|imperial]] counterparts, though definitions differ. The Mendenhall Order of 1893 redefined most units in terms of the meter and kilogram. Customary units are used in commerce and daily life, while science, medicine and much of industry rely on [[Metric system|metric]] units. The Metric Conversion Act of 1975 made the metric system "the preferred system of weights and measures for U.S. trade and commerce," but implementation has been limited.

Official currency of the United States and several other countries, subdivided into 100 cents. The Coinage Act of 1792 established the dollar as the base unit. Banknotes are issued as [[Federal Reserve]] Notes, popularly called greenbacks, and the Federal Reserve System conducts monetary policy. The dollar was originally defined in silver and, from 1834, in gold. It was linked solely to gold in 1900 and revalued to $35 per troy ounce in 1934, and all links to gold were repealed in 1971. After [[World War I]] it became an important reserve currency, and under the Bretton Woods Agreement near the end of [[World War II]] it displaced British sterling as the primary reserve currency. It is the most widely used currency in international transactions. As of January 1, 2025, about US$2.37 trillion in currency was in circulation.

Military intervention in [[Grenada]] led by the [[United States]] on October 25, 1983. It followed the execution of Prime Minister Maurice Bishop and the establishment of a Revolutionary Military Council under Hudson Austin. The invasion involved 7,600 troops, supported by Jamaican forces and troops of the Regional Security System, British prime minister [[Margaret Thatcher]] privately disapproved but supported the invasion publicly. A Security Council resolution deploring it was vetoed by the United States, and the General Assembly condemned it by 108 votes to 9. Coordination problems exposed during the operation prompted sweeping reforms under the Goldwater–Nichols Department of Defense Reorganization Act.

Declaration adopted by the [[United Nations]] General Assembly that codifies the rights and freedoms of all human beings. Drafted under the chairmanship of [[Eleanor Roosevelt]], it was adopted as Resolution 217 on December 10, 1948, in Paris, with 48 votes in favor, none against, eight abstentions and two not voting. Its 30 articles affirm "basic rights and fundamental freedoms" that are inherent, inalienable and universal, regardless of nationality, sex, religion or other status. Although not legally binding, it was the first step toward the International Bill of Human Rights, completed in 1966. Its principles have been incorporated into treaties and national constitutions, and it has been translated 577 times.

Dutch-American music corporation and the biggest music company in the world. It is one of the "Big Three" record labels, along with [[Sony|Sony Music Entertainment]] and Warner Music Group. Its name and logo originate from [[Universal Pictures]]. During [[World War II]], it donated more than 200,000 historic master recordings to the [[Library of Congress]]. [[Tencent]] acquired 10% of the company in March 2020 for €3 billion. It listed on the Euronext Amsterdam exchange in September 2021 at a valuation of €46 billion. As of April 2024, its catalog included over three million recordings and four million compositions.

American film production and distribution company, commonly known as Universal Studios. Founded on April 30, 1912, it is the oldest surviving film studio in the United States. It is the flagship of Universal Filmed Entertainment Group, part of [[NBC|NBCUniversal]], a subsidiary of [[Comcast]]. Founder Carl Laemmle began making films to avoid fees charged by the Edison-backed Motion Picture Patents Company, and he publicly credited performers, helping create the star system. Its mascot, Woody Woodpecker, was created by Walter Lantz.
